(a) adenoviral vectors trigger an inflammatory response in the vascular endothelium, (b) the inflammatory response causes endothelial injury, (c) the injury is reversible if inflammation can be prevented, and (d) the inflammatory threshold is much lower than previously believed.

(1) adenovirus causes an acute inflammatory response that is not necessary for transgene expression and (2) this acute inflammatory response causes endothelial dysfunction, which is also not necessary for transgenic expression.
acute injury after vascular gene transfer is caused by the host inflammatory response, and that this response can be prevented by making rabbits neutropenic with chemotherapy.

the development of gene therapy for the treatment of vascular disease.
the development of a new generation of adenoviral vectors that are less toxic to the vascular system and more suitable for gene therapy of vascular diseases.
the development of a novel approach for the treatment of peripheral arterial disease.

the inflammatory response is the primary cause of acute endothelial dysfunction after adenoviral vector gene transfer, and it is this endothelial dysfunction that is the primary cause for the poor transgene expression in vivo at high titers.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early inflammatory response is not necessary for gene expression, but that the inflammatory response is responsible for endothelial injury.
adenoviral gene therapy can be performed safely, but that titers should be kept below the threshold for acute inflammation and endothelial injury.
adenovirus-induced inflammation is a major cause of endothelial injury after vascular gene transfer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the acute inflammatory response to adenovirus is the major cause of endothelial injury, and this injury is mediated by neutrophils.
